title: Oriented diffusion tailors interfacial strain-polarization coupling for broadband electromagnetic absorption

paper_content.abstract: Repurposing the interfacial strain from a hindrance to synergism empowers critical advances for magnetoelectric composites in the application of next-generation energy storage and electromagnetic devices, by reconstructing the interfacial activity and local field distributions. However, its deterministic creation, pivotal for optimizing interfacial electron transport and emergent functionality, is impeded by the uncontrollable atomic distortion and arrangement. Here, we report an oriented-diffusion strategy that tailors interfacial strain by orchestrating atomic migration within a carbon-confined Fe3C/ZnO magnetoelectric heterointerface. Engineering the outward effusion of dielectric ZnO generates a progressive strain gradient, driving a transition in the interfacial strain from compressive to tensile prior to eventual relaxation. This programmed strain state reconfigures atomic-scale electric fields at the heterointerface, thereby enhancing electron transports and interfacial polarization properties. Consequently, this enhancement enables the strain-mediated metamaterial outperforms conventional electromagnetic absorbers, exhibiting an ultrabroad effective absorption bandwidth covers the wireless communication and radar stealth spectra (2.0-18.0 GHz) with an over 95% radiation reduction. These findings provide a novel perspective on deciphering strain-polarization coupling mechanism and guide the development of advanced broadband magnetoelectric functional materials.
paper_content.introduction:
With the rapid advancement and widespread adoption of Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), and smart mobile devices, the societal demand of wireless communication technologies has escalated to unprecedented heights1,2. However, less than 30% electromagnetic (EM) waves are utilized in telecommunication, the rest are largely ignored and wasted, constituting severe EM pollution in the surrounding environment and causing health concern and signal interference in electrical equipment3. EM absorption materials provide an effective solution to this issue by harvesting the EM wave and dissipating it into thermal energy. This fundamental energy-dissipation mechanism endows them with EM protection capability as functional fillers, enabling versatile applications that span from micro-nano high-precision electronics (such as on-chip components and integrated modules)4 to large-scale architectural infrastructures5, 6 (such as hospitals, laboratories, and transportation hubs) for industrial interference suppression and environmental shielding. Theoretically, the EM attenuation mechanism is mainly originated from the dielectric and/or magnetic dipoles of a material that interact with the radiation. To pursue superior absorption properties, considerable effort has been devoted to ingeniously integrating dielectric and magnetic components to achieve magnetic-dielectric coupling7. However, current research of magnetic/dielectric composites-based absorber attributes their synergistic effect to merely superimposing magnetic/dielectric contributions, ignoring the intrinsic interaction across the combined components8,9. Deciphering the potential magnetoelectric coupling mechanism for EM dissipation is heavily influenced by numerous factors (e.g., reasonable selection of materials system and systematical characterization), posing significant difficulty.

Designing magnetoelectric heterojunction is an effective approach to maximize the interaction between dielectric and magnetic components through a stable bonding at their contacted interface10. The heterogeneous interface, serves as a key mediator for magnetoelectric coupling, triggering distinctive interfacial effect such as built-in electric field, further contributing interfacial11, or dipoles polarization, internal scattering for EM dissipation12,13. Interfacial strain commonly exists in the magnetoelectric heterointerface owing to the formation of chemical bonds and electrostatic absorption across the interface14. Most reports roughly ascribe the contribution of strain for EM loss to dipole polarization induced by lattice defects and interfacial atoms rearrangement, while ignoring strain modulation towards the intrinsic electronic structure15. In certain dielectrics (e.g., piezoelectric, ferroelectric materials), residual static stress can trigger intrinsic electric polarization16, leading to energy band bending, barrier height modulation, and electron-hole compensation17. Zinc oxide (ZnO) exemplifies this class of functional dielectrics, exhibiting inherent piezoelectric and semiconductor properties18,19. Its pronounced high-temperature thermodynamic instability, which drives distinctive thermal diffusion behavior20, offers a practical pathway to leverage component rearrangement in designing interfacial interaction in the heterostructure systems. These findings establish magnetoelectric heterostructures as promising candidate materials for advanced electronic and spintronic applications, where interfacial strain can be regulated and potentially affect carrier transport efficiency. However, precise strain modulation at heterointerfaces, especially at the atomic scale, remains challenging. The difficulty mainly stems from the inherent lattice mismatch21, thermal expansion incompatibility22, and dynamic stress relaxation23 during material synthesis, compounded by a lack of visualized analysis regarding strains-induced electronic structure transitions at the heterointerface. These inabilities impose huge obstacles on understanding the relationships between microscale interfacial strain and macroscale EM properties, severely restricting the deterministic strain regulation (including strain types and gradient) and the development of advanced EM functional heterostructures.

In this study, we demonstrated a programmed strain-polarization coupling mechanism and fabricated strain-controllable magnetoelectric interfaces by controlling oriented diffusion in carbon confined heterostructures. The interfacial strain transitioned sequentially from compressive to tensile and finally to a relaxed state during the outward diffusion of ZnO. This strain evolution mediated a volcano-type profile in interfacial coupling strength by reconstructing the electronic field distribution. Remarkably, engineering tensile strain at the magnetoelectric heterointerface effectively enhanced the electron transport and amplified the built-in electric fields, boosting interfacial polarization relaxation to dissipate the incident EM wave. The strain-polarization coupled magnetoelectric metamaterial exhibits full-bandwidth (2-18 GHz) effective EM energy absorption, establishing it as a promising candidate for diverse applications in wide-frequency wireless communications and EM protection. Therefore, our work provided a novel method for designing magnetoelectric heterostructure with strong polarization responsiveness by leveraging interfacial strain, demonstrating significant potential for dual-use military and civilian applications.
paper_content.results:
Synthesis of confined magnetoelectric heterostructures
Confined ZnO/Fe3C magnetoelectric heterostructures were fabricated by precisely diffusing ZnO nanoparticles to a specific depth within carbon frameworks (Supplementary Fig. 1). As shown in Fig. 1a, this process initiated with the transformation of carbonaceous substrate tethered Zn/Fe oxide (ZFO) hybrids into carbon encapsulated ZnO/Fe3C yolk-shell nano-units through high-temperature carbothermal reduction, followed by manipulating the Zn source content for guiding the derivate ZnO effusion outwards the carbon nanocage. The carbon framework conversion from solid to yolk-shell was triggered by the Kirkendall cavitation effect24, causing the creation of limited nanovoid, as evident by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images (Supplementary Fig. 2). As Zn source content increased, excess ZnO gradually filled the surrounding voids, eventually breached the carbon cages confinement, and diffused outward to form continuous ZnO layers. Consequently, the ZnO/Fe3C (ZFC) heterostructure evolved through sequential confinement, penetration and separation stages with increasing ZnO content, as identified by high-resolution TEM (HRTEM), high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) elemental mapping (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. 3), with the corresponding specimens termed ZFC-1, ZFC-2, and ZFC-3, respectively. Additionally, the augmented ZnO content enhanced the carbothermal reaction, as evident by the thermal gravity analysis (TGA) and Raman spectra (Supplementary Fig. 4), further boosting the gradient outward diffusion process.

In addition to morphology analysis, we performed in-situ argon ion sputtering to progressively etch the outer ZnO layers of ZFC-3 to depths of up to 400 nm, thereby characterizing the outward diffusion affected component arrangements. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) depth profiling recorded both a gradual decrease in the intensity of characteristic Zn 2p peaks and an opposite trend in the Fe 2p signals (Fig. 1c), confirming the separation of ZnO and Fe3C during the enhanced effusion process. Concurrently, the reaction between carbon substrates and ZFO induced the chemical transformation from ZnFe2O4 into ZnO and Fe3C, resulting in the formation of an interface between ZnO and Fe3C within the magnetoelectric heterostructures. The phase evolution and chemical state variation was verified by X-ray diffraction (XRD), X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES), extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS), and XPS analysis (Fig. 1d-e, Supplementary Fig. 5-8 and Table 1). The absorption edge of Fe k-edge of ZFO and ZFC samples were close to that of Fe3O4 and Fe, respectively. In the Fe k-edge EXAFS of ZFO, a shift towards higher radial distance was detected in the peak of characteristic Fe-O-Fe, further identifying the formation of ZnFe2O4 in ZFO25. Meanwhile, the EXAFS of ZFC also confirmed the presence of Fe3C (via Fe-Fe and Fe-C peaks)26 and indicated the formation of interfacial chemical bonds in Fe3C/ZnO heterojunctions, as evident from emerging Fe-O peaks with a shift towards increased radial distance.

To reveal the configuration of the magnetoelectric interface built by semiconductor ZnO and ferromagnetic Fe3C, an aberration-corrected HAADF-STEM was employed to capture the ZnO/Fe3C heterostructures (Fig. 1f). Atomic arrangement of ZnO/Fe3C revealed a feature of coherent heterointerface, where the ZnO presented the (101) crystal plane and Fe3C exhibited the (211) crystal facet, thereby confirming atomically interactive connectivity across the interface. To minimize potential inaccuracies caused by closely spaced lattice, integrated differential phase contrast (iDPC) STEM was carried out. Detection of Fig. 1g presented a strong quantitative agreement between the crystalline structure and STEM results, accurately verifying the formation of magnetoelectric heterointerface between Fe3C (211) and ZnO (101). Additionally, the distribution of the intrinsic atomic-scale electric fields within Fe3C and ZnO were visualized using differential phase contrast (DPC) STEM27, with color vector wheels indicating the direction of the electric field (Fig. 1h). A uniform yet asymmetrical distribution of the local atomic electric field within each component reveals different potentials28, potentially inducing built-in electric field at the magnetoelectric interface.

Diffusion-regulated interfacial strain in confined ME heterostructures
To provide insights into the correlation between ZnO diffusion and magnetoelectric interface contact, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation (Supplementary Note 1) was employed to elucidate the ZnO content affected effusion process. The observations of recorded diffusion state indicated that at lower concentrations, ZnO molecules were largely hindered from penetrating the carbon layers (Fig. 2a). Conversely, with a higher initial concentration, the confinement imposed by the carbon layers was progressively overwhelmed, leading a pronounced outward diffusion. Continuous increase of the number density of penetrated ZnO (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 9) and the mean-square displacement (MSD, Fig. 2b) with the augmented concentration further proved the controllability of the ZnO gradient effusion process. In addition, ZnO oriented migration process inevitably affected the interface state, inducing potential reconfiguration of interfacial strain at the heterointerface. The interfacial stress field resulted from the ZnO gradient diffusion was characterized using geometric phase analysis (GPA) of STEM, complemented by strain distribution statistics (Fig. 2c-d and Supplementary Fig. 10). At the primary stage of magnetoelectric interface formation (ZFC-1), about 10.2% compression strains were detected at the ZFC interface, which was originated from the bonding effect of heterostructure formation. Upon initiation of ZnO outward diffusion (ZFC-2), the excess ZnO filled the original nanovoid within the carbon nanocages and tended to separate out, thereby inducing traction from the outer carbon layers on the penetrated ZnO. Concurrently, the upcoming separation of ZnO was also constrained by Fe3C owing to the interfacial bonding at the ZnO/Fe3C coherent heterojunctions and the static absorption, resulting in significant tension strain (16.8%) at their atoms contacted interface. The enhanced outward diffusion of ZnO overcame the constrains of both carbon shells and the interfacial bonding, thereby triggering the dissociation of the original ZnO/Fe3C heterointerface, as evident by the disappearance of Fe-O bond in Fe k-edge EXAFS of ZFC-3 (Supplementary Fig. 11). Seldom residual strain (0.5%) remained at the emerging Fe3C-C-ZnO triple-phase interface. Thus, the gradient-oriented diffusion process effectively governed a programmatic progression of the interfacial strain state from compressive to tensile, ultimately leading to its relief. The same interfacial strain states, with comparable quantitative values, was consistently observed in ZFC-x specimens across different batches (Supplementary Fig. 12), confirming the reproducibility and controllability of the oriented diffusion strategy.

To decipher the strain affected interfacial electronic structure, the distributions of interfacial electric field under different strain state were analyzed by the DPC-STEM technique (Fig. 2e). Unlike the uniform atomic electric fields in a homogenous component, pronounced distortion and mutual interaction were observed between neighboring Fe and Zn atoms across the interface, providing direct evidence of electric field couplings at the magnetoelectric heterointerface29. This atomic-level interfacial electric coupling was more pronounced as the compression strain converted to the tensile strain at the interface, which could accelerate the carriers transport across the interface and enhanced interfacial polarization. In contrast, only continuous and symmetrical atomic electric fields was observed within the separated ZnO, with no detectable electric field reconfigurations at the interface, implying the interfacial decoupling in ZFC-3 owing to the extinction of magnetoelectric heterojunction. In addition, the strain-mediated evolution of the interfacial coupling was analyzed using vector field distribution30 reconstructed from the atomic electric field maps (Fig. 2f). Characteristic gradients in the electric field vector rotation were detected at the magnetoelectric interfaces, confirming the strain-induced interfacial coupling. This coupling phenomenon was remarkably enhanced under tensile strain yet vanished upon interface separation. By precisely controlling ZnO diffusion to introduce interfacial strain, effectively programming the atomic electric field arrangement and the polarization capability at the magnetoelectric heterointerface.

Interfacial strain regulated electrical properties
The interfacial strain evolution guided by the gradient diffusion reconstructed the atomic interaction at the magnetoelectric heterointerface, varying the electrons motion in the interfacial built-in electric field (BIEF), thereby affecting the related electrical properties. Dielectric dispersion, manifested in frequency-dependent permittivity, fundamentally originated from the dynamic dielectric loss of absorbers to an external alternating electric field31. The variation of permittivity revealed that the interfacial strain enhanced dielectric dispersion properties, as verified by a steeper decline in permittivity with increasing frequency (Supplementary Fig. 13a-b) and a broader variation range across the 2–18 GHz band (Fig. 3a). This enhancement was mainly due to the strain-induced reconstruction of the local electronic structure via interfacial coupling (Fig. 2e-f), which accelerated realignment of interfacial potentials across the interface in response to the altering electric field, thereby improving interfacial polarization responsiveness32. The enhanced polarization relaxation could be characterized by the decreased real permittivity (ε′) and a more intense dielectric resonance peak in the imaginary part (ε″) for the strain-involved specimen (Supplementary Fig. 13a-b). According to the non-ideal Debye relaxation model33, the ε″, referred to the dielectric loss ability, was divided into conduction loss (ε″c) and polarization relaxation (ε″p) based on the tested electronic conductivity (Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 13c-d). Multiple polarization peaks were identified in the strain-involved ZFC heterostructures, and both of the peak intensity and width were increased as the interfacial state evolved from the relieved to compressive and tensile. This enhancement was also confirmed by the loss tangent of complex permittivity (tanδ = ε″/ε′), where the increased tanδ indicated the strain-improved dielectric loss ability (Fig. 3b). In addition, the interfacial strain affected polarization relaxation variation were analyzed by Cole-Cole plots. As the interfacial strain evolved from a relieved state to compressive and tensile states, the maximum relaxation peak shifted to higher frequencies (Fig. 3b), along with a broadened peak width (Fig. 3c). Theoretically, polarization relaxation peaks occurred when the frequency of the external electric field coincides with the intrinsic response rate (the reciprocal of the relaxation time) of the polarization mechanism within the absorbers34. Thus, this trend of relaxation peaks varied by the interfacial strain suggested a shortened relaxation time with a widened distribution35, demonstrating a sensitive yet broadband dielectric loss capability in the strain-involved magnetoelectric heterostructure.

To reveal the strain state-regulated interfacial polarization loss capability, off-axis electron holograms and projected charge density maps are conducted (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. 14). The red and bule regions in charge maps corresponded to the electronic depletion and accumulation, respectively, and the color depth reflected the charge density. The 3D charge density distribution of the strain-relieved interface exhibited flat distribution with weak intensity, ascribing to the decouple of the magnetoelectric interaction (Fig. 2f). In contrast, remarkable fluctuation characterized by the uneven arrangement of positive and negative charge were detected in the ZFC heterointerface with compression and tension strain. The increased potential differences implied the augmented absolute electronegativity across these coupled interfaces, which promoted interfacial polarization and its associated electric field energy dissipation. After a sequential process of Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), Inverse FFT (IFFT), filter method, the electron wave phases in the holograms were converted into electric potentials, finally the localized polarization intensity could be calculated based on the Poisson’s equations29. Fig. 3e illustrated that interfacial strain effectively elevated the polarization intensity, which could be further enlarged by the tensile strain owing to the accelerated electrons transport by the enhanced interfacial coupling. Additionally, the ε″p/ε″c value could reflect the contribution of polarization loss within the tested frequency range. As shown in Fig. 3f, the values of ε″p/ε″c ratio rise with increasing frequency, indicating that polarization loss played a more dominant role at higher frequencies. Notably, this frequency dependent enhancement was most significant in the ZFC-2 specimen with interfacial tensile strain, highlighting the controllability of polarization loss through strain engineering.

To deeply decipher the regulation mechanism of the polarization loss, the reconfigured electronic structures in the ZnO gradient diffusion controlled ZFC-based heterointerfaces were further theoretically analyzed by density functional theory (Supplementary Note 2). The projected density of state (PDOS) analysis revealed a gradient diffusion-induced reconstruction of interfacial electronic structures (Fig. 3g) and BIEF, consistent with the observation from the DPC and electron holography. As tensile strain was formed on the ZFC heterointerface, more pronounced orbits overlaps were detected, assigning to the enhanced interfacial coupling interaction, thereby boosting electron transports of the external electric field across the interface. As the interfacial strain state evolved from the relieved to compressive and tensile, the reduced work function (Φ) suggested the lowered energy barriers for charge migration (Fig. 3h and Supplementary Fig. 15), which improved the electron mobility and activity36. This improvement facilitated the supply of polarizable charges, thereby promoting the response of interfacial dipoles to external alternating electric fields. In additional, the differential charge density distribution revealed pronounced and inhomogeneous charge accumulation and depletion at these coupled magnetoelectric interfaces (Supplementary Fig. 16), forming multiple localized space-charge regions34. This result indicated the generation of robust interfacial dipole layers with a wide distribution37, which could account for broadening the distribution of polarization relaxation. Thus, these combined experimental results and theoretical analyses revealed a tunable strain-polarization coupling mechanism. The interfacial strain evolution, tailored by oriented diffusion, effectively orchestrated a reconfiguration of interfacial electronic properties via constructing interfacial coupling. This process created intense and wide-ranging polarization responsiveness, thereby significantly enhancing the dielectric loss performance in response to the external EM wave.

Application in EM wave absorption
Owing to the strain-tailored interfacial electric coupling effects and enhanced electric properties, the Fe3C/ZnO magnetoelectric heterostructures exhibited significant dielectric loss ability, showing potential application in efficient EM wave absorption. The strain-regulated EM absorption performance of the as-fabricated magnetoelectric heterostructures was evaluated, indexed by reflection loss (RL) and effective absorption bandwidth (EAB, frequency range of RL≤-10)38. In Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 17, both the minimum RL (RLmin) and maximum EAB (EABmax) exhibited the optimum when the magnetoelectric interface was subjected to tensile strain. A detail analyses of the EM parameters and magnetic response properties evolution (Supplementary Fig. 18-22 and Note 3) attributed this improvement to the increased dielectric loss ability caused by the strain-enhanced interfacial polarization and optimized impedance matching. The Fe3C/ZnO heterostructure within tensile strain exhibited a broad EAB of 7.38 GHz, covering entire Ku-band (from 12 to 18 GHz, the primary application band for radar stealth39), outperforming most reported EM absorption materials (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Table 3-4). Furthermore, we employed finite element analysis to simulate the surface current density and radar cross section (RCS) of a perfectly electric conducting (PEC) plate coated with ZFC-based magnetoelectric composites layers (Fig. 4c, Supplementary Fig. 23 and Note 4). Uniform distribution of surface current density40 and significant RCS reduction41 demonstrated the superior impedance matching and effective absorption properties of the strain-enhanced ZFC heterostructure in the simulated practical EM environment.

Widespread adoption of wireless communication techniques in civilian escalated the societal demand of absorbers with ultrawide EAB for addressing EM interference (produced by e.g., base stations, wireless routers and electronic devices)42,43. According to the equivalent medium theory, the periodic structure at subwavelength produced uniform EM response44. To achieve full-band absorption, an EM metamaterial was fabricated by mixing the strain-mediated Fe3C/ZnO heterostructures with resin and molding it into an 18 × 18 cm periodic metastructure (Supplementary Fig. 24 and Table 5), and the design principle of the metastructure were detailed in Supplementary Note 4. This hierarchical architecture, which featured pyramid-shaped units with internal perforation, could generate additional multiple resonances through impedance gradient matching and spatial dispersion. Fig. 4d showed the practical photos of the magnetoelectric metamaterial under the far-field testing environment. Remarkably, ultrawide EAB performance across the entire 2–18 GHz band was achieved, attributing to the synergistic effect between intrinsic excellent magnetoelectric coupling loss from heterostructures and diffraction resonances supplied by the metastructure.

To verify the application potential, we tested the absorption attenuation of the metamaterial against EM waves emitted by a 5G wireless router. Positioned as a shield in front of the WiFi router, the metamaterial remarkably reduced the detected radio frequency (RF) signals to the qualified levels (Fig. 4e). And the pronounced surface temperature elevation of the ZFC-2 metamaterials after radiation under a solid-state microwave source confirms the involved dissipation process from absorbed EM energy to heat (Supplementary Fig. 25 and Fig. 4f). Time dependent radiation values variation revealed that over 95% reduction of RF signals could be continuously achieved by this magnetoelectric metamaterials (Fig. 4g). In contrast, both control samples (the all-resin metastructure and the ZFC-2/resin plate) failed to achieve effective EM attenuation (Supplementary Fig. 26), further demonstrating that the impressive EM protection arises from the synergistic contribution between the strain-mediated magnetoelectric absorbers and the designed metastructure. Additionally, the corresponding dissipation mechanism was investigated via finite element simulation45. The frequencies (5.8 and 14.0 GHz) of characteristic resonance peaks identified from the RL results were selected to elucidate the EM field response behaviors. As shown in Fig. 4h, the attenuation of low-frequency EM energy occurred primarily through magnetic field dissipation, while at high frequencies it is dominated by electric field dissipation. This frequency-dependent behavior was confirmed by the spatial overlap of electric/magnetic field distributions and energy loss profiles46. These inspiring findings demonstrated that the tensile strain-enhanced magnetoelectric heterostructure provided a promising sustainable solution to address the elevating EM interference.

In conclusion, we have successfully fabricated carbon confined ZnO/Fe3C magnetoelectric heterostructures, and precisely tailored the interfacial strain by controlling the oriented diffusion gradient. As the strain of the magnetoelectric heterointerface evolved from the compressive to the tensile and relieved, the interfacial atomic electric fields exhibited an evolution from the enhanced interfacial coupling to the decoupling. Furthermore, the strain-driven coupling effect reconfigured the electronic structures across the atomic heterointerface, effectively accelerating the interfacial electrons transport and broadening the distribution of interfacial dipoles, thereby enhancing the polarization relaxation response ability. Eventually, the tensile strain-enhanced magnetoelectric heterostructure performed impressive EMA properties with a broad EAB covered 7.38 GHz; and its derivate metamaterials achieved full-band efficient absorption (2-18 GHz) and over 95% radiation attenuation efficiency, exhibiting significant potential for dual-use civilian and military application. Our results proposed a novel mechanism of interfacial strain engineering in regulating electronic properties and broaden the design paradigm of advanced EM functional materials.
paper_content.methods:
General
The chemicals, electromagnetic parameters measurement, molecular dynamics simulation, and density functional theory are given in the Supplementary Methods and Notes.

Synthesis of ZnO/Fe3C@C-x (ZFC-x)
ZFC-x microspheres were prepared by continuous spray drying and annealing treatment. First, 3.0 g PVP-K30 and 0.9 g TMA was dissolved in of a 60 mL solution composed of isometric DI water, anhydrous ethanol, and DMF under vigorous stirring to obtain a homogenous solution. Then, 2.0 mmol Fe(NO3)3∙9H2O, x mmol Zn(NO3)2∙6H2O were simultaneously added into the solution and stirring until dissolution. The final obtained yellow spray solution was fed into a spray dryer, and the spray drying parameters were an inlet temperature of 180 °C, outlet temperature of 90 °C, feed rate of 1500 mL h−1, and an atomization pressure of 0.4 bar. The collected spray dried precursors were pre-treated at 300°C for 60 min to obtain solid ZFO@C hybrids, followed by pyrolyzing at 600 °C under N2 atmosphere for 300 min at a heating rate of 2 °C/min to obtain the ZFC-x. In addition, the ZFC-x samples prepared at the Zn(NO3)2∙6H2O amount of 1.0, 3.0, and 5.0 mmol were denoted as ZFC-1, ZFC-2, and ZFC-3, respectively.

Fabrication of ZFC based EM metamaterials
ZFC-based metamaterials with a size of 18 × 18 cm within periodic aligned units were prepared via a moulding process, the geometric parameters of the as-designed metamaterial unit were listed in Supplementary Table 5. First, a rubber inverted mold template was obtained via 3D printing. Then, a certain amount of ZFC powders were added into a fresh prefab resin mixture (the added weight ratios of resin E51, curing agent, and accelerator were 14:5:1) with a weight ratio of 2:3 and violently stirred for 30 min. The as-obtained ZFC/resin mixtures were poured into the 3D-printed inverted mold template and degassed for 60 min under the vacuum ambient. The inverted mold template with the degassed ZFC/resin mixtures were transferred to an oven and cured under 80 ºC for 12h. After the completion of curing, the final ZFC-based EM metamaterial was obtained.

Characterization
Field-emission SEM images were obtained using a Hitachi S-4800 microscope. TEM, HRTEM, EDS mapping results and off-axis electronic holography results were obtained on a on a dual spherical aberration correction field-emission STEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Spectra 300 TEM, American) operated at 300 kV, equipped with STEM-iDPC detector, STEM-HAADF detector, and Super-X EDS. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were recorded on a Bruker-Axe X-ray diffractometer equipped with a Cu Kα radiation source (λ = 1.5406 Å, 40.0 kV, 40.0 mA). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) results were analysed on a Thermo Scientific ESCALAB 250Xi spectrometer equipped with a monochromatic X- ray source and argon etching system. X-ray absorption fine structure spectra were collected at the RapidXAFS 2M (Anhui Absorption Spectroscopy Analysis Instrument Co., Ltd.) by transmission mode at 20 kV and 40 mA. All spectra were collected in ambient conditions. Raman spectroscopy measurement was performed on a Renishaw inVia spectrometer under a 633 nm laser excitation. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA, PerkinElmer) was performed in an air atmosphere to evaluate the content variation. The conductivity of the samples was tested by analysis of a four-point probe surface resistance tester.

Data Availability
Source data are provided with this paper. The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon request.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript titled “Oriented atomic diffusion tailors strain–polarization coupling for broadband electromagnetic absorption” presents a technically robust strategy to modulate interfacial strain for achieving broadband electromagnetic (EM) wave absorption. The authors construct ZnO/Fe₃C@C microspheres (ZFC–x) featuring gradient tensile–compressive strain fields induced by controlled outward ZnO diffusion during annealing. The study effectively integrates advanced characterization techniques such as aberration-corrected STEM, electron holography, and XANES/EXAFS with multiscale simulations to elucidate the correlation between atomic-scale strain evolution, polarization relaxation, and interfacial charge transfer.

The central innovation lies in transforming interfacial strain from a passive structural feature into an active tuning parameter for dielectric and magnetic losses, thereby achieving a high effective absorption bandwidth of 7.38 GHz at 2.2 mm, further extendable to full 2–18 GHz coverage in a resin composite. The work is scientifically sound and presents clear potential for practical applications in EM interference mitigation. It can be considered suitable for publication in Nature Communications after the authors satisfactorily address the following critical points.
1. The rationale for selecting ZnO in the heterostructure should be clearly mentioned.
2. In the DFT methodology, the DFT+U approach is generally required for Fe-containing systems, but the manuscript does not specify the Hubbard U parameter; this should be clarified.
3. The authors should specify whether a high-spin or low-spin configuration and what kind of magnetic interactions were considered in the DFT simulations.
4. The choice of (211) and (101) crystal planes for Fe₃C and ZnO, respectively, in the DFT models should be justified.
5. In the XPS analysis, O 1s and C 1s spectra should be included alongside Fe and Zn, and the Fe 2p spectrum should be deconvoluted to show multiplet splitting.
6. The Fe 2p XPS (Fig. 1c) and Raman (Supplementary Fig. 4b) spectra exhibit a relatively low signal-to-noise ratio; improved data quality is recommended.
7. Supplementary Figures 10 and 12 can be merged for conciseness.
8. The Cole–Cole plots should be fitted using an appropriate equivalent circuit model to substantiate relaxation behaviour.
9. Extracted parameters from Rietveld refinement should be provided to validate structural claims.
10. The synthesis relies on precise ZnO outward diffusion and strain balancing; therefore, the manuscript should discuss reproducibility across batches and potential challenges in scaling up the process for industrial production.
11. Long-term stability under cyclic heating or humid conditions should be examined, as Fe₃C and carbon shells may degrade upon oxidation.
12. While qualitative relationships between strain, dielectric loss, and absorption are established, quantitative correlations would greatly strengthen the mechanistic understanding.
13. A comparison table contrasting EAB, reflection loss, and filler loading with representative Fe-, Co-, and Ni-based hybrid absorbers would help contextualize the performance gains.
14. The introduction briefly discusses EM pollution, but a more concrete discussion of practical applicability, such as the feasibility of large-scale EM shielding in industrial or architectural contexts, would make the work more relevant.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In the manuscript "Oriented Atomic Diffusion Tailors Strain-Polarization Coupling for Broadband Electromagnetic Absorption," the authors explore interfacial strain engineering to enhance the electronic properties of electromagnetic materials. They created a carbon-confined Fe3C/ZnO magnetoelectric heterointerface, where varying Zn precursor content influences the effusion of ZnO through the interface, leading to carbon-encapsulated yolk-shell nanostructures. The strain transition from compressive to tensile alters interfacial atomic electric fields, shifting from enhanced to decoupled coupling. This strain effect modifies the electronic structures, improving polarization relaxation and electron transport. The resulting heterostructure exhibited impressive electromagnetic absorption properties, with a broad effective absorption bandwidth of 7.38 GHz and an over 95% radiation attenuation efficiency from 2 to 18 GHz.
This work significantly expands the design framework for advanced electromagnetic functional materials. The authors have thoroughly studied their samples and provided both theoretical simulation and application-based evidence to support their claims.
However, there are a few questions to consider before publication.
1. With the increase of ZnO diffusion, a variation in carbon shell thickness from ~635 nm to ~860 nm to ~270 nm is observed in the ZFC-x samples. Please explain why this large variation is observed.
2. The x-axis in Fig. 3f represents discrete ZnO samples; however, the graph displays a continuous 2D plot. Please clarify how this graph is created.
3. The authors state in lines 339-340 that they tested the electron conductivity (σ) of the samples using a four-probe measurement. Based on this conductivity (σ), they categorized the dielectric loss (ε′′) into conduction loss (ε ′′) and polarization relaxation (ε ′′). However, they did not provide any details or data regarding this measurement.
4. The VNA typically provides S-parameters. What method is used for converting these S-parameter data into intrinsic sample parameters, such as permittivity and permeability?
5. Additionally, in the equations for input impedance and reflection (Equations 6 and 7 in the supplementary materials, lines 46 and 47), it appears that a constant term related to the free space impedance (Z ) is absent.
6. The authors developed an electromagnetic (EM) metamaterial by combining a strain-mediated Fe C/ZnO heterostructure with resin, molding it into an 18 × 18 cm periodic metastructure to achieve full-band absorption. However, the rationale behind selecting this specific metastructure and how its dimensions were determined remains unclear. A brief explanation of the reasoning behind this choice would be beneficial for the article.
There are also a few typing and grammatical errors in both the main article and the supplementary article. The annotated documents highlighting these errors are attached for consideration.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this paper, the authors propose a new method for designing yolk-shell composite nanoparticles with controllable interfacial strain between the two components. They demonstrate it by synthesizing ZnO/Fe3C nanoparticles, where magnetoelectric interface forms through the outward diffusion of the ZnO species from the Zn + Fe + O + C precursor mix. Further, they investigate the evolution of the microstructure and macroscopic properties of these nanoparticles with the change of Zn/Fe precursor ratio. With theoretical calculations (molecular dynamics) and experimental data, the authors show, that the strain at the interfaces changes from compressive to tensile and then to neutral (relaxed) with increasing Zn content, and that the interfaces with tensile strains can be efficiently used as a GHz radiation absorber.
Overall, the article presents a very comprehensive and topical study with clear applications and therefore can be published in Nature Communications. However, several issues should be addressed before publication:
1. SEM images (supplementary Fig 2) show, that the size of the nanoparticles vary greatly, but I could not find any information about the average size or the size distribution for different ZFC powders. Fig 1b also features spherical particles of different size. Particle size is directly related to the magnetoelectric interface area to volume ratio, so it may skew the measured macroscopic parameters of the samples. I would like the authors to provide some statistical data on the ZFC powders morphological parameters and to comment on the relations between these parameters and the measured permittivity and GHz absorbing capabilities.
2. The comparison (Fig 4b and supplementary Table 1) with other microwave absorbing materials is lacking. For example, there are articles, reporting materials with better EAB at lower or similar thickness, such as FeCo-Ti3C2 MXene (EAB – 8.8 GHz at 1.6 mm thickness, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmmm.2019.165639), ZF/rGO aerogels (EAB – 8.4 GHz at 2.1 mm thickness, https://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4414816) and SiO2@FCIP + MWCNT (EAB – 7.9 GHz at 1.9 mm thickness, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compositesa.2025.108719). While the parameters, obtained in the current manuscript are impressive, they can not be called record-breaking. I would like the authors to expand the comparison with these and/or other reports to make it more balanced.
3. Vertical axis break and change of scale in Figure 4b is misleading. I can not find a good reason to make it this way. Please, remove the line break or explain why it is necessary.
4. Figures 4e and 4f show, that GHz radiation from a consumer grade WiFi router heats the shielding resin metastructure up to 45 oC in one minute. It is hard to believe, considering very low peak RF power density of 150 mW/m2 (Fig 4g). By my estimations even if the metastructure dissipates all of the RF radiation into the thermal energy, in one minute it could only heat up by less than 1 oC (or heat up a very thin < 1 mkm surface layer by 20 degrees). I would like the authors to clarify the thermal balance of this experiment.
5. I could not find detailed information about the molecular dynamics simulation neither in the main text, nor in the supplementary notes. I would like the authors to provide a description of the initial state used in the simulations and how different ZnO concentrations were implemented.
6. How the statistical data on Supplementary Fig. 8 were gathered? From the text it is not clear, if it is a strain distribution within a single heterointerface or a distribution of average strains of several interfaces? In my understanding, big part of the theoretical considerations in the manuscript rely on the results, presented in Supplementary Fig. 8, so I would like the authors to provide evidence, that these strain distributions are representative.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
A magnetoelectric Fe3C/ZnO composite and its heterointerface were analyzed in detail, showing the redistribution of interfacial strain and polarization fields. It is shown that the polarization fields are strong when interfacial strain is large and that this causes high dielectric loss. The authors demonstrate the properties of the strained heterointerface in an EM absorption experiment, showing wideband absorption. The authors use a suite of advanced analysis tools to demonstrate the interfacial properties of the heterointerface but the basic theory and physical principles behind the wideband absorption is not immediately clear.
While the results are nice, polarization control for EM absorption has already been extensively studied in all types of forms of 2D TMCs, nanoparticles, composites, defects, etc. In this context, the novelty of the work is not remarkably persuasive. The physical aspects how it can be differentiated from those of other works should be elucidated very clearly.
1. Please add classic references that link interfacial polarization to EM wave absorption.
2. Pg. 6 Clarify which ZnO crystal plane is being analyzed. In one place it says (101). In another it says (111).
3. In Figures, it is hard to tell without labels which figure refers to ZFC1, 2 and 3. (Figure 1b, 2a, 2c, etc)
4. It’s hard to understand the plot in Figure 3a. The text says that this is a dispersion curve, but there is no spectral data. What do the range of values refer to?
5. Pg. 8 “THe dielectric dispersions arise from an electronic reconfirugration triggered by atomic-level stress regulated interfacial potential difference”. This is a general statement and can apply to any variation in the dielectric dispersion. Can the authors be more specific?
6. Pg. 8, In the loss tangent plot, the authors describe a polarization relaxation peak. Specify its location. Can its origin be clarified using the analysis before (eg. Why does it occur at the specified frequency. What is the physical reason?)
7. Pg.9 ‘THe polarization enhancement, becoming more remarkable as the frequency moved to the higher band’. This sentence is hard to understand
8. If the goal is to show the properties of the composite in the EM absorption demonstration, it would be more convincing to perform the experiment on a film instead of a metasurface. Otherwise, it is hard to tell if the performance enhancement and wide-band absorption properties is due to the metasurface or the intrinsic properties of the composite. The relative contributions of the two effects are not explained in the current form.
9. Please clarify the physical principles that link the unique interface strain engineering to wide-band absorption.

General Response: We thank the reviewer for their careful reading of our manuscript and for noting that our work presents clear potential for practical applications in EM interference mitigation.
Q1: The rationale for selecting ZnO in the heterostructure should be clearly mentioned.
Response 1: We wish to clarify that the core rationale for selecting ZnO in our Fe C/ZnO magnetoelectric heterostructure is fundamentally rooted in its exceptional and tunable dielectric properties and thermal diffusion behaviors. On the one hand, its dielectric behavior is mainly originated from the wurtzite crystal structure of ZnO, which features alternating layers of Zn2+ and O2- ions stacked along the c-axis, creating an intrinsic dipole moment and superior response ability toward external electric field [Ref. R1-2]. This unique atomic arrangement facilitates multiple polarization mechanisms [Ref. R3-4]: electronic polarization from its wide bandgap, strong ionic displacement polarization due to the charged sublattices, and defect-related relaxation polarization, which makes it as a promising dielectric candidate for electromagnetic wave absorption [Ref. R5]. Additionally, potential piezoelectric property of semiconductor ZnO can be harnessed to effectively regulate the interfacial electronic structure and polarization behaviors [Ref. R6, 7] by inducing tunable strain at the Fe C/ZnO magnetoelectric interface.
On the other hand, owing to the thermodynamic instability of ZnO under low oxygen partial pressure and elevated temperature [Ref. R7], an appropriate high-temperature thermal treatment can trigger the generation and outward migration of highly mobile zinc species in the composite system [Ref. R8]. Consequently, the distribution of ZnO can be effectively tailored by manipulating reaction parameters during this distinctive thermal diffusion process, enabling the targeted precise modulation of interfacial interaction in our fabricated Fe C/ZnO magnetoelectric heterostructure. These properties are pivotal for achieving enhanced and tailorable interfacial polarization response behaviors and electromagnetic absorption performance.

Q2: In the DFT methodology, the DFT+U approach is generally required for Fe-containing systems, but the manuscript does not specify the Hubbard U parameter; this should be clarified.
Response 2: Thank you for this insightful comment. We fully agree on the necessity of the DFT+U approach for correctly describing the localized 3d electrons in our Fe C-involved system. In our calculations, we employed the PBE+U method, with an effective Hubbard U parameter of 4.0 eV applied to the Fe 3d orbitals. This choice of U = 4.0 eV is based on its established use in prior DFT studies on similar iron carbides [Ref. R1-2], where it has been shown to provide a balanced description of the electronic structure, magnetic properties, and stability. These details are also supplemented in the Supplementary Notes 2: Density function theory calculation.

Q3: The authors should specify whether a high-spin or low-spin configuration and what kind of magnetic interactions were considered in the DFT simulations.
Response 3: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding the magnetic configuration. In DFT simulation of the Fe C/ZnO heterostructure, the magnetic ground state of Fe C 3 3 was carefully considered. Based on established literature [Ref. R1], Fe C adopts a ferrimagnetic ordering 3 as its ground state, with local magnetic moments on Fe atoms approximately around 2.0 μB. Accordingly, in our fabricated models, the initial magnetic moments for each Fe atom were set to 2.0 μB, corresponding to a high-spin-like configuration consistent with its metallic character and previous studies [Ref. R1- 3]. ZnO was treated as non-magnetic initially. The calculations were performed using spin-polarized DFT+U (PBE+U) with an effective Hubbard U = 4.0 eV applied to the Fe 3d orbitals to better account for on-site electron correlations [Ref. R4]. Throughout the structural relaxation of the heterojunction, all atomic positions and the supercell were fully optimized while allowing the magnetic moments and ordering to relax freely. This approach ensures that our model not only starts from a physically justified magnetic state but also self-consistently converges to the lowest-energy magnetic configuration of the interface system.

Q8: The Cole–Cole plots should be fitted using an appropriate equivalent circuit model to substantiate relaxation behavior.

In the frequency region corresponding to the strongest dielectric relaxation peaks detected in the tan plots (Fig. 3b), conduction loss and polarization loss jointly contributed to the overall dielectric lo 𝛿 ss𝜀 ability (Supplementary Fig. 13c-d). Thus, the equivalent circuit model comprises three parallel branches (Response Fig. 1): a high-frequency capacitance (C ) branch representing the instantaneous polarizations and providing the ∞ baseline dielectric value for all relaxation processes, a leakage resistance (R ) branch accounting for leak the ohmic loss due to electronic conductivity, and a relaxation branch formed by a series combination of a resistor (R ) and a capacitor (C ) to model the dielectric polarization loss [Ref. R1-3]. The R is 1 1 leak dominated by the intrinsic electronic conductivity of sample, thus, the increased R well accounted leak for the weakened conduction loss ability of the ZFC-x samples (from ZFC-1 to ZFC-2 and ZFC-3). In addition, the combination of resistor and capacitor governs the relaxation time (τ) and its corresponding characteristic frequency (ƒ), which are associated with the polarization responsiveness and the location r of the strongest dielectric loss peak, respectively. The gradually shortened τ from ZFC-3 to ZFC-1 and ZFC-2 revealed the accelerated polarization relaxation response, while the shift of the ƒ towards the r higher frequency was in accord with the variation of strongest dielectric loss peaks observed in the tan plot, indicating the rationality of the fitted equivalent circuit models. 𝛿𝜀
In the relaxation branch, the R and C represent the energy dissipation rate and the charge storage 1 1 capacity, respectively, associated with a specific polarization process. In the interfacial polarization dominated ZFC heterostructures, the value of R and C could reflect the potential barriers for electron 1 1 to cross the interface and the amount of the transported electrons [Ref. R3-4]. As the interface strain was implemented and evolved to the tensile strain (from ZFC-3 to ZFC-1 and ZFC-2), the increased capacitance of the C suggested the accumulation and depletion of more electrons on the heterointerface, 1 while the decreased R suggested the reduced interfacial barriers. These enhancements were well 1 assigned to the boosted electron transfer from the interfacial coupling (Fig. 2e) and increased interfacial charge density differential (Fig. 3d), respectively, demonstrating that interfacial strain could effectively accelerate the relaxation kinetics by promoting the interfacial polarization.

Q10: The synthesis relies on precise ZnO outward diffusion and strain balancing; therefore, the manuscript should discuss reproducibility across batches and potential challenges in scaling up the process for industrial production.
Response 10: Thanks for your valuable comments. We wish to clarify that the ZnO/Fe C 3 magnetoelectric heterostructure with controllable interfacial strain is fabricated by a scalable spray-pyrolysis method. And the gradient ZnO outward diffusion and corresponding interfacial strain are precisely controlled by a ZnO content guided dynamics process, as evident by the theoretical molecular dynamics simulation (Fig. 2a-c and Supplementary Note 1) and series of microstructure characterization (Fig. 2d-e and Supplementary Fig. 10). As suggested, we have supplemented three batches of three distinct ZFC-x samples and carried out a systematic microstructure characterization, including the HRTEM and corresponding GPA, on the interfacial strain state to further verify the reproducibility of ZnO outward diffusion-driven interfacial strain modulation. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 12a, three supplemented ZFC-1 batches present a remarkable compressive strain concentration on the contacted magnetoelectric interface, which are well consistent with the compression state in the manuscript-mentioned ZFC-1 interface (Fig. 2c). Similarly, both of the tensile state in ZFC-2 interface and the relieved state in ZFC-3 are further confirmed by the supplemented several heterointerface regions (Supplementary Fig. 12b-c), demonstrating that the reproducibility and representativity of the qualitative determination of these heterointerface states. Regarding the quantitative relation, although there are slight fluctuations in the average values of these interfacial strain (ε ), most ε values locate in an acceptable error range, xy xy and the whole averaged values of all measured ε are – (11.2 2.0) %, (13.7 3.2) %, and – (0.25 0.6) % in ZFC-1, ZFC-2, and ZFC-3, respectively. These repeatability verification results convincingly evidence the feasibility and effectivity ± ± ± of interfacial strain state regulation by controlling ZnO outward diffusion gradient.

As shown in Response Fig. 3d, all specimens except the one treated at 300 °C exhibited similar permittivity profiles to that of the pristine ZFC-2, with fluctuations below only 8%. Q12: While qualitative relationships between strain, dielectric loss, and absorption are established, quantitative correlations would greatly strengthen the mechanistic understanding.
Response 12: Thanks reviewer for the recognition on our established relationships between strain, dielectric loss, and absorption. We wish to clarify that the motivation of this work is to design functional magnetoelectric heterostructure with tunable strain state of interface by a facile strategy of manipulating the ZnO oriented diffusion gradient. Systematical structure characterizations based on advanced electronic microscopy technologies (such as aberration-corrected atomic resolution STEM, DPC and electron holograms) combine with multidimensional theoretical simulations reveal that the diffusion-driven interface strain evolution can effectively reconfigure the interfacial electric field coupling behaviors, which further tailors the polarization ability and the eventual optimization of electromagnetic absorption properties.
Achieving quantitative correlations between interfacial strain and polarization, the present interfacial strain engineering driven by gradient oriented diffusion remains challenge. The difficulty stems not only from the inherent complexity of the magnetoelectric interface but also from the pronounced size effects and potential quantum responses in the composite nanomaterials system [Ref. R1,2]. Different from the monodispersed nanocrystal heterostructures with uniform size [Ref. R3,4], the sizes of our fabricated Fe C/ZnO magnetoelectric heterostructures mainly located in a controlled range of 3 10~60 nm (Supplementary Fig. 2c). The dominance of surface atoms in these relatively fine particles and the size-dependent electronic structure collectively give rise to a strain field that is highly sensitive to minuscule variations in morphology and composition, eventually resulting in a ranged fluctuation of interfacial strain values [Ref. R5-7]. Nevertheless, our proposed oriented diffusion strategy could qualitatively program the interfacial strain state, evolving from the initial compression to tension and terminal relaxation as the ZnO outward diffused to the outer. Remarkably, specimens from different batches also consistently exhibited the same interfacial strain state (such as compressive strain in ZFC-1, tensile strain in ZFC-2, and relieved strain in ZFC-3), as evident by the HRTEM images and corresponding GPA results (Supplementary Fig. 12), confirming the semi-quantitative controllability of magnetoelectric interfacial strain state regulation. Unlike previously reported magnetoelectric composite nanoparticles, which primarily focused on material fabrication with limited tunability, our strategy of semi-quantitative interfacial strain modulation offers an effective pathway to bridge strain-polarization coupling by programming the interfacial contact behavior between the dielectric and magnetic components. And we found that the interfacial strain state evolution effectively tailored the polarization relaxation time. Specifically, the relaxation time shortened as strain implemented due to faster electron transport and wider interfacial dipoles distribution mediated by enhanced interfacial coupling, thereby enhancing the polarization responsiveness and dielectric loss ability towards the incident EM wave (Fig. 2 and 3). Eventually, the magnetoelectric heterostructure composite with interfacial strain exhibited the enhanced broadband absorption performance (Fig. 4a). Therefore, such a constructed investigation network from microscale materials design to atomic scale mechanism deciphering and macroscale performance controllability has provided a significant guidance for developing advanced EM absorption materials.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In the manuscript "Oriented Atomic Diffusion Tailors Strain-Polarization Coupling for Broadband Electromagnetic Absorption," the authors explore interfacial strain engineering to enhance the electronic properties of electromagnetic materials. They created a carbon-confined Fe C/ZnO 3 magnetoelectric heterointerface, where varying Zn precursor content influences the effusion of ZnO through the interface, leading to carbon-encapsulated yolk-shell nanostructures. The strain transition from compressive to tensile alters interfacial atomic electric fields, shifting from enhanced to decoupled coupling. This strain effect modifies the electronic structures, improving polarization relaxation and electron transport. The resulting heterostructure exhibited impressive electromagnetic absorption properties, with a broad effective absorption bandwidth of 7.38 GHz and an over 95% radiation attenuation efficiency from 2 to 18 GHz. This work significantly expands the design framework for advanced electromagnetic functional materials. The authors have thoroughly studied their samples and provided both theoretical simulation and application-based evidence to support their claims. However, there are a few questions to consider before publication.
General Response: We thank the reviewer for their careful reading of our manuscript and for noting that our work significantly expands the design framework for advanced electromagnetic functional materials.
Q1: With the increase of ZnO diffusion, a variation in carbon shell thickness from ~635 nm to ~860 nm to ~270 nm is observed in the ZFC-x samples. Please explain why this large variation is observed.
Response 1: We wish to clarify that the measured thickness of ~270 nm corresponds to the effused ZnO layers on the ZFC-3 sample (the inset of Supplementary Fig. 2b), which is well confirmed by the HRTEM results of the ZnO lattice on the outer wrinkled surface (Supplementary Fig. 3c). The overall carbon framework evolves from a hollow structure with a carbon shell in ZFC-1 and ZFC-2 to a solid structure coated with ZnO layers in ZFC-3 as the ZnO diffusion gradient increased till the eventual effusion (Supplementary Fig. 2b). This carbon structure evolution from hollow to solid spheres can be attributed to the interplay between the Kirkendall effect and precursor concentration. At lower metal salt concentrations (ZFC-1), the outward diffusion of metal species during annealing surpasses the inward diffusion, leading to vacancy accumulation and the formation of a hollow cavity (Kirkendall effect) [Ref. R1-2]. Due to the low concentration, the outward diffusion of metal species lacks sufficient driving force to breach the outer carbon layer, resulting in their confinement within the carbon matrixes (ZFC-1). As the ZnO concentration increases, the increased metal flux and concomitant carbon redistribution widen the metal/carbon interfacial region [Ref. R3], making the carbon shell appear thicker, as evident by the increased carbon shell thickness from ~635 nm to ~860 nm. The outward diffusion, promoted by the higher ZnO concentration, manifests as distinct bulges on the surface of the ZFC-2 microspheres. Ultimately, as the concentration increased to cause effusion of ZnO (ZFC-3), the excessive metal species fill the interior nanovoids (Supplementary Fig. 2c), suppressing the Kirkendall effect and leading to the formation of a densely solid composite architecture. Meanwhile, the higher concentration increases the nucleation site density, which promotes the coalescence of outwardly effused ZnO nuclei into continuous wrinkled layers rather than discrete bulges.

Q6: The authors developed an electromagnetic (EM) metamaterial by combining a strain-mediated Fe C/ZnO heterostructure with resin, molding it into an 18 × 18 cm periodic metastructure to achieve 3 full-band absorption. However, the rationale behind selecting this specific metastructure and how its dimensions were determined remains unclear. A brief explanation of the reasoning behind this choice would be beneficial for the article.
Response 6: Thanks for the reviewers’ reasonable comments. We wish to clarify that the design of this periodic metastructure aims to broaden the EAB ranging from 10.62 to 18.00 GHz in original strain-mediated Fe C/ZnO heterostructure (ZFC-2) to the full-band frequency (2-18 GHz) absorption. 3 According to the equivalent medium theory, the periodic structure at subwavelength (for example, the wavelength at the frequency range of 2-18 GHz decreased from 15.0 to 1.67 cm) can produce uniform electromagnetic response [Ref. R1]. And the design principle of such a pyramid-like metastructure for broadband EM absorption lies in impedance gradient matching and spatial dispersion of resonant frequencies. The tapered geometry creates a transition in effective impedance from the tip (near free-space) to the base (near the substrate), which minimizes reflection at the air-material interface, allowing waves to enter efficiently. Simultaneously, different heights of the structure resonate at different frequencies, and these multiple resonances spatially overlap and merge, resulting in a continuous, ultra-wide absorption band [Ref. R2-4]. Different from the conventional solid pyramid structure, an internal perforation is set in the periodic unit (Supplementary Fig. 24), which can act as resonators for inducing additional localized resonances that synergize with the primary pyramid's gradient. This perforation can effectively broaden the absorption bandwidth, particularly extending performance toward lower frequencies. Meanwhile, strategic porosity significantly reduces the material's areal density while largely maintaining its external electromagnetic profile, achieving crucial weight savings for practical applications [Ref. R5-6]. Based on these considerations, an innovative metastructure is developed, as characterized by pyramid-shaped periodic units with a perforated architecture. Then, the involved dimensions for this proposed periodic metastructure were precisely optimized by a series of reflection loss (RL) simulations in the tested frequency region of 2-18 GHz using the EAB as the objective function. Eventually, the as-present ZFC-x based metamaterial with specific dimensions was deterministically fabricated, as evident by the geometry parameters varied 1D RL profiles Response Fig. 4. Revision in the manuscript: Supplementary Note 4: Electromagnetic simulation and metamaterials design. The design principle of such a pyramid-like metastructure for broadband EM absorption lied in impedance gradient matching and spatial dispersion of resonant frequencies. The tapered geometry created a transition in effective impedance from the tip (near free-space) to the base (near the substrate), which minimized reflection at the air-material interface, allowing waves to enter efficiently. Simultaneously, different heights of the structure resonated at different frequencies, and these multiple resonances spatially overlapped and merged, resulting in an ultra-wide absorption band24. Different from the conventional solid pyramid structure, an internal perforation was set in the periodic unit (Supplementary Fig. 24), which could act as resonators for inducing additional localized resonances that synergize with the primary pyramid's gradient. This effectively broadened the absorption bandwidth, particularly extending performance toward lower frequencies25. This strategic porosity significantly reduced the material's areal density while largely maintaining its external electromagnetic profile, achieving crucial weight savings for practical applications. And the involved dimensions for this proposed periodic metastructure were optimized by a series of reflection loss (RL) simulations in the tested frequency region of 2-18 GHz using the effective absorption bandwidth (EAB) as the objective function. Eventually, an innovative metastructure was developed, characterized by pyramid-shaped periodic units with a perforated architecture. (Page 9 in revised Supplementary Materials)

In this paper, the authors propose a new method for designing yolk-shell composite nanoparticles with controllable interfacial strain between the two components. They demonstrate it by synthesizing ZnO/Fe C nanoparticles, where magnetoelectric interface forms through the outward diffusion of the 3 ZnO species from the Zn + Fe + O + C precursor mix. Further, they investigate the evolution of the microstructure and macroscopic properties of these nanoparticles with the change of Zn/Fe precursor ratio. With theoretical calculations (molecular dynamics) and experimental data, the authors show, that the strain at the interfaces changes from compressive to tensile and then to neutral (relaxed) with increasing Zn content, and that the interfaces with tensile strains can be efficiently used as a GHz radiation absorber. Q1: SEM images (supplementary Fig 2) show, that the size of the nanoparticles vary greatly, but I could not find any information about the average size or the size distribution for different ZFC powders. Fig 1b also features spherical particles of different size. Particle size is directly related to the magnetoelectric interface area to volume ratio, so it may skew the measured macroscopic parameters of the samples. Response 1: Thanks for the reviewers’ reasonable considerations on the microsphere sizes distribution, we strongly agree with the reviewers’ point on the relation between microscale particle size and macroscopic parameters. To address the mentioned size variation in the original Supplementary Fig. 2a, we have resupplied the larger-horizon SEM images of the spray-drying prepared spherical precursors and their derivate ZFC-x products, and the size distribution statistics of spraying-dried precursors, ZFC-x microsphere and involved nanoparticles are also summarized in the revised Supplementary Fig.2.
Firstly, we wish to clarify that the microspheres size fluctuation is mainly attributed to the intrinsic properties of spray-drying preparation technology, which firstly nebulize the precursor solution into numerous droplets with a certain size ranging and then evaporate the involved solvent by contacting with the input high-temperature flows, eventually obtaining the dried spherical powders with a normal size distribution [Ref. R1-3].
In this work, our motivation is modulating the magnetoelectric interface strain by controlling a ZnO content driven gradient outwards diffusion process, and the materials systems are prepared via spray-drying and post pyrolysis treatments. As shown in the Supplementary Fig. 2a, all spray-dried precursors possessed a spherical structure with a close average size of 2.55 0.05 um, demonstrating the slight effects of variate Zn source content on the size distribution. After the subsequent heat ± treatment of these precursors, the ZFC-x microspheres were yielded, and the corresponding spherical sizes were reduced owing to the pyrolysis of carbon-based matrixes in precursors. Even if the involved ZnO content were different, the overall size distributions of ZFC-x microspheres still maintained a close average values (Supplementary Fig. 2b), indicating that the morphology size might not be the dominated factor on the variation of permittivity and absorption performance in this work. As for the inside nanoparticles, potential particles aggregation might exist due to the inward contraction of carbon framework from the ZnO outward diffusion (the inset in Supplementary Fig. 2b), but majority of nanoparticles presented similar sizes with an average value slightly ranging from 23.10 nm to 25.02 nm, and 24.44 nm (Supplementary Fig. 2c). The similar and close size distributions in both of the overall microspheres and nanoparticles among the three as-fabricated ZFC-x samples revealed the slight effects of varied ZnO content on the size, further confirming that the size effect played limited roles in the variation of measured permittivity and absorption capability along the diffusion gradient.

Specifically, we optimized the gradient evolution in the diffusion models and refined the simulation steps to have a clearer understanding on the ZnO-concentration dominated outward diffusion process. Prior discussions demonstrated that the ZFC heterostructure composites is converted from the carbon nanocages confined ZFO hybrids via carbothermal reaction, resulting in the formation of nanoporous on the carbon substrate [Ref. R1], as evident by the HAADF-STEM results (Supplementary Fig. 2). Additionally, during the high-temperature carbothermal process, the metal species can catalyze the graphitization of the surrounding carbon matrixes [Ref. Based on the primary experimental observation, the initial state of ZFC-x composite systems with different ZnO concentrations was modeled, and the description is below:
Three ZFC-x systems with different ZnO content shared a common layered architecture. From the bottom to the top of the simulation box, the structure comprised a porous graphene layer, a layer of iron carbide molecules, a layer of zinc oxide molecules, two porous graphene layers, and a vacuum region. The relative pore offset between the two porous graphene layers was 0.1 nm. The three systems differed in the number of zinc oxide molecules, where the numbers of zinc oxide molecules in ZFC-1, 2, and 3 were 12, 24, and 36, respectively. Each system was first subjected to energy minimization, followed by simulations in the NVT ensemble at 873.15 K with a time step of 0.5 fs for a total duration of 10 ns. Temperature was controlled using the V-rescale thermostat. During the simulations, all components except the ZnO molecules were kept fixed to preserve the structural framework. Additionally, the MD simulation details (including the modeling of initial states and the simulation methods) and the corresponding analyses are supplemented into the revised Supplementary Note 1 and manuscript, respectively.

Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
A magnetoelectric Fe C/ZnO composite and its heterointerface were analyzed in detail, showing the 3 redistribution of interfacial strain and polarization fields. It is shown that the polarization fields are strong when interfacial strain is large and that this causes high dielectric loss. The authors demonstrate the properties of the strained heterointerface in an EM absorption experiment, showing wideband absorption. The authors use a suite of advanced analysis tools to demonstrate the interfacial properties of the heterointerface but the basic theory and physical principles behind the wideband absorption is not immediately clear. While the results are nice, polarization control for EM absorption has already been extensively studied in all types of forms of 2D TMCs, nanoparticles, composites, defects, etc. In this context, the novelty of the work is not remarkably persuasive. The physical aspects how it can be differentiated from those of other works should be elucidated very clearly.
General Response: We thank the reviewer for their careful reading and noting that our results are nice. We agree with the reviewer's pointed the feasibility on regulating EM absorption via polarization control. However, majority of current researches merely remain superficial methodologies explorations, mainly relying on ambiguous phenomenological descriptions (such as simple components optimization, dimension and microstructure design, and uncontrollable defects introduction), lacking deep and novel insights into the correlation between microscale polarization regulation mechanism and macroscale EM absorption performance. A fundamental yet crucial limitation is the lack of high-precision, visualized identification for the sources of induced polarization within materials, coupled with the absence of a finely programmable strategy for their precise modulation. This gap in mechanistic insight significantly hinders the development of advanced polarization loss-dominated EM absorbers.
To tackle these bottlenecks, our research aims to address it through several key innovations:
(i) Deterministic fabrication of magnetoelectric heterostructure composite with adjustable interfacial strain state
In this work, we proposed an oriented diffusion strategy to construct atomic interfacial strain in magnetoelectric heterostructures. The interfacial strain states evolved from compression to tension and relaxation could be precisely programmed by manipulating the diffusion gradients, which was verified through theoretical simulation and experimental observation. This approach capitalized on the intrinsic thermodynamic properties of dielectric component ZnO itself, distinct from the additional composition and structural modifications, or external fields assistance required in conventional strain engineering.
(ii) Atomic-level visualization on the strain-reconstructed interfacial coupling and electronic structure variation
Advanced electron microscopy characterization and analysis techniques (including DPC, iDPC, electronic hologram) were utilized to visualize variations in interfacial electronic properties under different strain states. Our observations unveiled a strain-induced atomic-level electric field coupling on the magnetoelectric heterointerface, along with a notable enhancement of this coupling upon the application of tensile strain. The interfacial coupling, verified by DFT calculations, increased atomic-scale orbital overlaps and reduced the work function, which accelerated carriers migration across the interface and enhanced the interfacial built-in electric field.
(iii) Decipherment of the correlation between interfacial strain-polarization coupling mechanism and broadband EM absorption
Systematic analysis of dielectric properties and theoretical calculation demonstrated that strain-induced interfacial electronic coupling effectively modified the polarization kinetics by shortening relaxation time and broadening the distribution, thereby enhancing the dielectric loss capability. This mechanism, distinct from reported strategies that rely solely on lengthening relaxation time, highlighted the role of strain-polarization coupling. Eventually, the broadened dielectric loss combined with optimized impedance matching jointly endowed the magnetoelectric heterostructures with a broadband EM absorption performance.
(iv) Practicability demonstration of strain-engineered magnetoelectric metamaterials with excellent EM protection
Leveraging the synergy between the strain-broadened interfacial loss mechanism and the metastructure design, the optimized tensile-strain-engineered magnetoelectric metamaterial achieved remarkable full-band (2~18 GHz) electromagnetic wave absorption and attenuated incident radiation by over 95%. These results demonstrated its promising potential for application in civilian EM protection, and provided significant guidance for developing advanced composite material systems with wideband EM absorption.
In addition, we have addressed the reviewer’s comments, especially, deepened the physical mechanism analysis for clearer understanding of the strain-polarization coupling correlation. The point-to-point responses are detailed as below:

Zhang et al. [Ref. R2] revealed the significance of interfacial polarization in the core/shell structure composite nanoparticles for improving EM wave absorption performance. Cao et al. [Ref.
